title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Share a width-tapered combinational divider across RV32M operations
motivation:
The baseline's worst timed path crosses forwarding and the ALU, reaching
199.837 ns through 156 cells at a median Fmax of 5.442 MHz. alu.sv expresses
DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU as separate signed/unsigned division and remainder
operators. Their combinational implementation is the strongest suspected
source of the deep arithmetic path and substantial LUT usage. A smaller,
explicitly shared divider can improve the timed circuit even when CoreMark
is executing other operations, because the full RV32IM hardware is timed.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only the real DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU datapath with one combinational
unsigned restoring divider that produces quotient and remainder together.
Keep the existing pipeline, forwarding and bus-handshake behavior, with
no extra cycles for any instruction. For signed operations, convert both
operands to unsigned 32-bit magnitudes before the divider, then negate the
quotient when operand signs differ and negate the remainder only when the
dividend is negative. Unsigned operations use the original operand bits.

Make the 32 unrolled restoring stages explicitly width-tapered. At stage
k=1..32, append dividend bit 32-k to the previous remainder to form a
k-bit trial remainder. Subtract divisor[k-1:0] once using a k+1-bit
zero-extended subtraction. Accept its low k bits and set quotient bit
32-k only when the subtraction has no borrow and every divisor bit above
k-1 is zero; otherwise retain the trial remainder and emit quotient zero.
At k=32 the upper-divisor predicate is constant true. Use the subtraction's
borrow bit instead of a separate magnitude comparator, and use static
generate widths so early stages contain only the necessary carry logic.
The final stage supplies both results; do not infer another '%' circuit.

Preserve division-by-zero results explicitly (quotient 0xffffffff,
remainder original dividend) and signed INT_MIN/-1 results (quotient
0x80000000, remainder zero). Keep the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitutions
exactly as they are and exclude the real divider from that build. Keep
multiply and all RV32I datapaths unchanged. The expected gain comes from
sharing arithmetic, reducing carry-chain width and avoiding duplicate
comparator/subtractor logic, with unchanged iterations per cycle.

title: Move division out of the single-cycle execute path
motivation:
The only recorded bench experiment is the baseline: 5.442 MHz with a
199.837 ns worst path spanning forwarding, EX, and the combinational ALU
through 156 cells. There are no previous structural attempts or recorded
lessons. The ALU implements signed and unsigned divide and remainder with
combinational / and % operators. These unrolled arithmetic networks remain
in the timed result-selection cone even when an ordinary RV32I instruction
executes. Moving this rare, deep operation behind registers offers much
more timing headroom than improving an individual forwarding mux.

The only recorded bench experiment is the baseline: 5.442 MHz with a
199.837 ns worst path spanning forwarding, EX, and the combinational ALU
through 156 cells. There are no previous structural attempts or recorded

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace all four combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU paths with one shared,
blocking, iterative divider connected to EX. Keep RV32I execution and
multiplication on their existing single-cycle paths. The divider captures
the fully forwarded operands and operation exactly once, converts signed
operands to unsigned magnitudes, and performs one radix-2 restoring
division step per cycle using a registered partial remainder, quotient,
divisor, and a bounded counter. Share the magnitude datapath between signed
and unsigned operations and between quotient and remainder; register sign
correction before presenting the result. A normal division takes about
34-35 cycles including preparation and completion. Explicitly implement
divide-by-zero and signed INT_MIN/-1 semantics with bounded early finish.

While the divider runs, hold the instruction in ID/EX and stop fetch/decode,
but let older EX/MEM and MEM/WB instructions drain. Insert invalid bubbles
into EX/MEM rather than freezing an already completed memory request or
replaying an older retirement. Clear reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, and
redirect controls in these bubbles as well as valid, because the current
memory and forwarding logic consumes control bits without validity gates.
An older dmem stall still holds EX/MEM and
takes precedence over divider issue and result transfer. Latch forwarded
operands at accepted launch so draining WB cannot change an active divide.
Retain an unconsumed registered result until EX/MEM can accept it, transfer
it exactly once with the original instruction's RVFI metadata, then resume
the pipeline. Preserve the existing EX/MEM and MEM/WB forwarding priority;
the completed divide result uses the normal EX/MEM forwarding path for its
dependent successor. Gate divider launch and result transfer with valid
instruction and pipeline-accept conditions, and cancel internal state on
reset. No memory request, redirect, or retirement is generated by divider
busy bubbles.

Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, keep the exact existing per-operation stand-in
formulas and compute them from the captured operands in a short two-cycle
divider transaction through the same launch, busy, drain, and held-result
control. This exercises the new interlock within the fixed formal depth
instead of making all divide retirements unreachable within that depth.
Apply the stand-ins to all operands, including zero and overflow cases;
the real build must contain no combinational / or % datapath.
Preserve nret=1, all core ports, decoder legality, trap handling, and the
existing memory-handshake contract. The prediction is that removing the
dominant division cone raises Fmax far more than the occasional extra
divide cycles reduce CoreMark iterations/cycle. Validate that tradeoff with
the existing marker-bounded CoreMark run and Gowin timing after implementation.

title: Small tagged target predictor eliminates recurrent control-flow bubbles
motivation:
The baseline always fetches pc+4 and redirects in EX for every taken
conditional branch, JAL, or JALR. Since IF/ID is combinational rather
than a separate register, each redirect discards one younger instruction
and inserts a bubble. CoreMark repeatedly executes loops and stable
direct jumps, so many of these bubbles should be predictable. The sole
recorded experiment has 4,491,485 measured cycles and 5.442 MHz median
Fmax. Its critical path runs through forwarding and the combinational
arithmetic unit, so this proposal targets iterations per cycle while
keeping predictor logic small enough to avoid reducing Fmax. There are
no recorded predictor experiments or LESSONS.md takeaways in this fixture.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 64-entry direct-mapped branch target buffer with an integrated
two-bit saturating direction counter. Index with fetch PC[7:2]; retain
the full PC[31:8] tag, a word-aligned 30-bit target, a conditional versus
unconditional type bit, and a valid bit. A matching unconditional entry
predicts its cached target; a conditional entry predicts that target
when the counter MSB is set. A miss or not-taken prediction chooses pc+4.
Include JAL and JALR in the same predictor, using the last resolved
target for JALR, without adding a return stack or global history.

Carry the exact predicted next PC alongside each accepted instruction
through IF/ID and ID/EX. In EX compute the architectural next PC using
the existing forwarded operands, branch comparison, JALR bit-zero
clearing, and misalignment/trap rules. Redirect and flush only when a
valid instruction advances out of EX and its actual next PC differs
from its saved prediction. Check this equality for every instruction,
including non-control and trapped instructions, so stale entries cannot
silently skip architectural instructions. RVFI pc_wdata always reports
the resolved next PC, never the prediction. Correctly predicted taken
control flow captures the target instruction normally without a bubble.

Train once per valid EX advance, never during dmem holds or bubbles.
Allocate only decoded legal control-flow instructions with aligned
targets; initialize conditional counters to weakly taken or weakly
not-taken according to the resolved direction, and saturate on later
tag-matching updates. Unconditional entries always predict taken and
update their target on each resolution. Invalidate a matching stale
entry when a non-control instruction or trapping control flow resolves
there. Clear valid bits on reset; other table fields need not reset and
must be ignored when invalid. Use a compact asynchronous-read,
synchronous-write table rather than a fully associative search.

Preserve the existing bus and load-use protocol: a prediction advances
the fetch PC only when the current instruction is accepted; imem stalls,
load-use stalls, and dmem holds keep the PC and any held prediction
metadata stable. Defer EX correction and training while dmem holds EX;
on release, correction overrides imem/load-use holds and squashes the
younger instruction. Predictor reads must be independent of flush and
stall outputs to avoid a combinational feedback loop. Preserve MEM/WB
forwarding retention, architectural side-effect suppression, all trap
checks, and the existing nret=1 IO and retirement-order contract.

The predicted benefit is approximately 8% higher fitness from avoiding
recurring control-flow bubbles, assuming approximately unchanged Fmax.
Counter aliasing, changing JALR targets, and FPGA table routing are the
main uncertainties. Validate with directed retirement/side-effect tests,
the existing formal and cosimulation gates, canonical CoreMark CRCs and
MMIO timing brackets, and the evaluator's median Gowin Fmax times
iterations/cycle. This is a predictor-only change; retain the arithmetic
implementation, memory interfaces, and pipeline register boundaries.

title: Remove redirect-driven payload muxes from fetch and decode
motivation:
The registered divider champion scores 101.21 at 45.46 MHz, with a
27.6 ns worst path through ID, EX, IF, hazard logic, and back to ID.
Its predecessor's combinational-divider micro-optimization regressed;
division is already off the ordinary execute path in this source.
Currently EX redirect forces the combinational fetched instruction to
NOP before register-file addressing and immediate/decode logic, and
ID flush clears every bit of the wide ID/EX payload. This places late
branch resolution on wide decode data and register-enable paths.

The registered divider champion scores 101.21 at 45.46 MHz, with a

Its predecessor's combinational-divider micro-optimization regressed;

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Narrow pipeline squashing to validity and control state without changing
stage boundaries, instruction latency, or the one-bubble EX redirect
policy. Have if_stage always expose the raw imem_data instruction and
current PC; flush, redirect, and unavailable instruction memory affect
only out.valid. Preserve redirect-over-stall PC update priority.

Split the ID/EX sequential update into payload and control updates.
Reset payload fields normally, but after reset capture PC, instruction,
immediates, operand data, register addresses, and destination whenever
!stall, independently of flush and in.valid. On stalled cycles retain
these payload fields. Separately clear valid and the entire ctrl_t on
reset or flush, with flush retaining its current priority over stall.
When !stall and no flush, capture in.valid and capture decoded controls
only if in.valid; otherwise capture ctrl_t='0. Clearing controls as well
as valid is essential because downstream forwarding and memory logic
consume some controls without validity qualification. Squashed payload
values are ignored until a later accepted instruction overwrites them.

Keep the hazard unit's raw source-address dependency comparisons
independent of redirect and flush. Do not gate load-use detection with
if_id.valid, because that validity contains redirect and would route
branch resolution back to the payload register enable. A real redirect
comes from a branch or jump in EX, so id_ex_mem_read is false and raw
wrong-path source bits cannot introduce a load-use hold on that cycle.
If imemReady is low while a load is in EX, a dependency in unavailable
raw imem_data can only request the bubble already required for the
missing instruction; preserve the existing dmem-hold and EX-busy priority
so an older stalled memory operation or active divide is never lost.

This removes the redirect-to-NOP mux before both register-file read
addresses and decode, and removes redirect flush from the wide ID/EX
payload D/enable cones. The expected gain is higher median Gowin Fmax
with unchanged CoreMark iterations/cycle. Keep the registered divider,
ALTOPS arithmetic, forwarding priority, decoder default-illegal checks,
alignment traps, nret=1 IO, and retirement ordering intact. Verify exact
retirement and memory side effects under coincident redirects and bus
stalls, then use canonical marker-bounded CoreMark and vendor timing
to establish whether fitness exceeds the 4.6 percent acceptance margin.

title: Register the fetch-to-decode boundary to break redirect feedback
motivation:
The iterative-divider champion reaches 101.21 fitness at 45.46 MHz,
with 4,491,817 marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. Its reported worst path
is now 27.6 ns through 47 cells, from the register file to an ID/EX
operand register through ID, EX, IF, and hazard logic. The nominal
IF/ID bundle is actually combinational: EX redirect selects a NOP
onto the live instruction bus, changing decode and register-file read
addresses before the same edge captures ID/EX. This creates a long
backward control path through a second operand-read cone. The previous
structural attempt successfully removed division from ordinary timing;
retain that improvement and cut this newly exposed pipeline path.

The iterative-divider champion reaches 101.21 fitness at 45.46 MHz,
with 4,491,817 marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. Its reported worst path
is now 27.6 ns through 47 cells, from the register file to an ID/EX
operand register through ID, EX, IF, and hazard logic. The nominal
IF/ID bundle is actually combinational: EX redirect selects a NOP
onto the live instruction bus, changing decode and register-file read

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Turn the combinational IF/ID bundle into a one-entry registered,
elastic fetch-to-decode stage carrying instruction, its exact PC, and
valid. Decode and both register-file read addresses must depend only
on the registered instruction, never on a combinational redirect,
bus-ready signal, or injected NOP. Keep ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB, the
existing forwarding paths, and the blocking iterative divider. This
is one structural change: establish a real register boundary between
instruction fetch and decode to sever the redirect-to-decode feedback.

Use explicit consume and refill events. A buffered instruction is
consumed only when decode can advance without a load-use interlock,
dmem hold, divider occupancy, or redirect. When the slot is empty or
is being consumed, a ready instruction-memory response may refill it
on the same edge; advance the fetch PC by four exactly on that refill.
When full and blocked, retain the buffered PC/instruction and fetch PC.
When empty, allow a refill even if downstream is blocked. io_imemReady
qualifies only new fetch acceptance: a buffered instruction remains
available to decode even if the instruction bus subsequently stalls.
If decode consumes without a refill, clear buffer valid and inject
subsequent invalid bubbles rather than replaying that instruction.

Keep raw registered instruction payload independent of squash. On an
accepted EX redirect, set fetch PC to the resolved target, invalidate
IF/ID and the younger ID/EX instruction, and suppress same-edge refill
from the old fetch address. Redirect overrides fetch backpressure;
EX must still defer resolution while an older dmem operation holds it.
The target is fetched on a later ready cycle. Both younger slots must
be killed, including when the buffered wrong-path instruction is a

title: Instruction-qualified direction prediction with short recovery control
motivation:
The divider champion scores 101.21 at 45.46 MHz, with a 27.6 ns worst
path crossing ID, EX, IF, the hazard unit, and ID again. Fetch currently
chooses pc+4 for every instruction. Every taken branch or jump discards
one younger instruction, and EX redirect also masks the entire fetched
instruction to a NOP before decode and register-file reads. The previous
64-entry tagged target predictor reduced marker-bounded CoreMark cycles
from 4,491,485 to 4,197,517, but was evaluated on the old combinational
divider and therefore did not challenge the current champion. That is
evidence for predictable control flow, not evidence that its large
target table or full next-PC comparison is the best implementation here.
A direction-only predictor can remove recurring direct-control bubbles
while keeping prediction storage and correction control small.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one instruction-qualified direct-control predictor to the existing
single-issue divider champion. Use a 128-entry, two-bit saturating branch
history table indexed by PC[8:2], initially weakly not taken. Predict a
conditional branch taken from its counter MSB, predict every aligned JAL
taken, and leave JALR sequential for its existing EX resolution. Qualify
prediction with the current raw instruction: BRANCH opcode and valid
funct3, or JAL opcode, plus a word-aligned direct target. Compute the
B/J target from the current PC and sign-extended immediate in IF. Compute
direct_target and pc+4 in parallel with the direction-table read, then
select between completed addresses; do not place the counter read or
prediction decision before a carry chain. There is no cached target,
PC tag, global history, or return stack. Aliasing
affects direction accuracy only; a table entry cannot redirect a load,
store, illegal encoding, or other non-control instruction.

Carry the exact predicted-taken bit and the computed direct target with
the accepted instruction through IF/ID and ID/EX. Direct branch and JAL
targets in EX use that instruction's saved target, with existing trap
checks and RVFI next-PC semantics preserved. Since a predicted direct
target is derived from the same instruction, correct direct predictions
require only a direction XOR rather than comparing two 32-bit next PCs.
Define actual_nonsequential as a valid, legal, aligned taken branch or
jump. Correct when actual_nonsequential differs from saved predicted
taken; an aligned JALR always requires correction because it is never
predicted. On a predicted-taken branch that resolves not taken, recover
to pc+4, not the branch target. Suppress direct prediction for a target
with bit 1 set; a taken misaligned branch or jump still traps using the
existing rules, with sequential architectural next PC and no link write.
RVFI reports resolved pc_next and architectural operands, never a guess.

Make predictor recovery squash through ID/EX valid and control clearing
at the register boundary. Keep IF/ID instruction bits and register-file
read addresses independent of EX correction: remove the redirect/flush
NOP mux on the fetched instruction, but still invalidate an unavailable
or squashed fetch. ID must capture an all-zero bubble on a flush or an
invalid input, clearing reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, and branch/jump
controls as well as valid. Existing memory and forwarding logic consumes
some controls without valid gates, so clearing valid alone is unsafe.
Give correction explicit priority over the younger raw instruction's
load-use indication. Compute hazard decisions from raw instruction bits
and independent interlock signals so correction cannot feed back through
instruction masking or fetch validity. This removes the existing
forwarded-branch-result to fetched-instruction to decode-data path;
correction remains a register squash and PC-select control signal.

Update conditional counters exactly once when a valid legal aligned
branch advances from EX to EX/MEM, including both taken and not-taken
outcomes. Do not train during reset, bubbles, divider occupancy, or dmem
holds. Use the saved prediction actually selected on fetch acceptance,
not a fresh table lookup in EX. On load-use, divider, and dmem holds,
keep PC and the held instruction's prediction metadata; during imem
not-ready, emit an invalid input and do not advance PC or fabricate a
retirement. A ready EX correction overrides imem/load-use stalls and
kills the younger instruction. Defer correction while dmem holds EX.
Correctly predicted taken branches and JALs accept the target instruction
normally. Preserve divider launch/held-result behavior, MEM/WB forwarding
retention, nret=1 ports, memory handshakes, decoder legality, and order.

The expected gain is about 12 percent in fitness from fewer direct-control
bubbles and a shorter recovery cone. The main uncertainty is whether
fetched-instruction predecode plus the direct-target adder becomes a new
Gowin critical path; keep the counter read, target adder, and correction
selection shallow and inspect vendor timing. Validate marker-bounded
CoreMark with canonical CRCs and the existing formal/cosim gates. Judge
the proposal by median Gowin Fmax times iterations/cycle against 101.21;
a cycle reduction alone is insufficient, and acceptance requires more
than 4.6 percent improvement over that champion.

title: Share all RV32M multiply results through one signed 33-bit product
motivation:
The champion scores 115.00 at a median 48.328 MHz. Its 27.223 ns
worst Gowin path starts at the register file, traverses operand
selection and the signed multiplier, and passes through multiple
result-selection LUTs before reaching the data-memory address port.
A fresh placement-option-0 timing run confirms mul_ss_63_s0 is on
that path. The ALU currently computes three separate full products
for signed/signed, unsigned/unsigned, and signed/unsigned operations;
the timed design uses six DSP blocks. Earlier micro_opt attempts
addressed division and redirect feedback, not this multiplier cone.
A local prototype of the proposed change reduced DSP usage to two
and produced Gowin Fmax values of 54.198, 55.939, and 55.939 MHz
across the three scored placement options. The median is 15.75 percent
above the champion's, providing evidence beyond placement noise.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the three combinational multiplication expressions in alu.sv
with one explicitly sized signed 33-by-33 multiplier shared by MUL,
MULH, MULHU, and MULHSU. Preserve zero-cycle ALU latency and the
existing pipeline, forwarding priority, branch prediction, divider,
bus handshakes, and single-channel RVFI interface.

Form signed 33-bit operands A={sign_a,a} and B={sign_b,b}.
sign_a is a[31] only for MULH or MULHSU, otherwise zero; sign_b is
b[31] only for MULH, otherwise zero. Declare both operands and the
66-bit product signed, with explicit widths so expression sizing
cannot truncate the multiply. A leading zero makes every unsigned
RV32 operand a nonnegative signed 33-bit value, while the replicated
sign bit preserves a signed RV32 operand exactly. MUL selects
product[31:0]; all three high-half operations select product[63:32].
Product bits [65:64] are redundant extension bits and are unused.

Decode signedness in parallel with operand routing and change only
the extra operand bits; do not add full-width magnitude conversion,
operand negation, or subtractive high-half correction. Group the
three high-half case labels onto the same result wire so the M-result
selection contains only low versus high selection, followed by the
existing ALU operation selection. Keep one multiplication expression
in the real build, allowing Gowin to infer a shared DSP datapath and
remove duplicated multiplier inputs and result-selection branches.
The gain should come from lower operand fanout, fewer DSP blocks,
and a smaller result mux, with identical CoreMark cycle count.

Keep every RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS operation-specific XOR formula exactly
unchanged; guard real multiplier declarations and logic outside that
build. Preserve all ordinary integer operations and inactive real
DIV/REM ALU outputs. Maintain decoder legality and all trap behavior.
Validate all four actual multiply operations, including sign extremes,
and run unchanged formal and stalled cosimulation/CoreMark gates.
The local prototype passed the existing ALU and pipeline suites plus
4,784 additional exact multiply checks with successive operation
changes, both unstalled and stalled selftest RVFI cosimulation, and
stalled CoreMark with all canonical CRCs and no out-of-bounds access.
CoreMark's marker-bounded cycle count stayed exactly 4,202,272.
Compare median vendor Fmax times marker-bounded iterations/cycle
against 115.00; acceptance requires fitness above 120.29. The prototype
projects 133.12 iter/sec, a 15.75 percent improvement. Its option-0
worst arrival fell from 27.223 to 23.745 ns. Preserve the tested narrow
sign-bit selection and shared high-half result to reproduce this
mapping; branch recovery is now close to the remaining multiplier
path and limits the scope for further gains from this local change.

title: Register fully bypassed operands before execute
motivation:
The champion scores 115.00 at a median 48.328 MHz with 4,202,272
marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. A fresh make timing TARGET=bench run
reproduces its placement-option-0 Fmax of 45.603 MHz. The full Gowin
report identifies a 27.223 ns path from the register-file BSRAM output
through ID operand logic, EX forwarding, ALU input selection, the
signed multiplier DSP, and result selection into the dmem address.
A nearly tied 27.150 ns path starts at the other register-file BSRAM
output, crosses the same EX forwarding prefix, then branch comparison
and correction into the fetch-PC enable. Isolating only multiplication
would therefore leave another limiting path. The previous IF/ID
register experiment added branch refill cycles for a modest timing
gain. The more promising structural boundary is between operand
acquisition/bypass and execution, shared by both limiting paths.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Retime the bypass network across the ID/EX operand registers. Resolve
architectural source values and ALU input selection in ID, then
register the final values that EX will consume. EX reads those registers
directly instead of muxing raw register-file values with EX/MEM and
MEM/WB results immediately before arithmetic and branch comparison.
Keep the existing instruction-stage count, single-cycle non-divide
execution, blocking divider, load-use bubble, and direct predictor.
This is one structural change to operand/result flow, not a new fetch
stage or a separate multicycle-multiply proposal.

For an instruction admitted from the combinational IF/ID payload,
select each source with youngest-writer priority: the current advancing
EX instruction's architectural result, then the current completing
MEM instruction's architectural result, then the existing write-first
register-file read (which already incorporates WB). Compare source
addresses with the producer destinations, require nonzero destinations
and valid eligible register writes, and hardwire x0 to zero regardless
of bypass matches. The current EX producer supplies its resolved ALU
or multiply result, PC+4 link value, or accepted divider response.
It is eligible only when it can actually advance, is not a load, and
its final trap-adjusted controls permit the write. Export this value
before the EX/MEM register hold/bubble mux. The MEM producer supplies
its ALU result or correctly extracted/sign-extended load result, and
is eligible only on completion with a permitted register write. A
stalled or misaligned load must never forward its address or invalid
read data as a register value. WB remains the oldest candidate through
the register file's existing same-cycle bypass.

Capture the selected rs1/rs2 values as the architectural operands in
ID/EX. Also capture explicit alu_a and alu_b fields there, selecting
PC for AUIPC and the immediate for immediate-source instructions in
ID rather than leaving these muxes in front of the EX arithmetic.
Keep both architectural rs values for branch comparison, JALR,
store data, divider requests, and RVFI; ALU input selection must not
replace the architectural operand metadata. EX's ALU uses only the
registered alu_a/alu_b, while its other consumers use the registered
rs1/rs2. Preserve the saved direct target and prediction metadata.
The resulting dependency recurrence is registered operands -> EX
arithmetic -> younger ID bypass selection -> registered operands.
There is no combinational path from younger decode operands back into
the executing instruction. A dependent ordinary ALU or multiply can
still issue each cycle, because it captures the older EX result at
the same edge that the older instruction enters EX/MEM. This moves
operand selection after computation and makes the execution sources
explicit flops instead of a register-file-BSRAM output followed by
forwarding. It shortens both the DSP and branch-recovery timing cones.

Preserve one bubble for an immediately dependent load. While the load
is in EX, its result is unavailable: hold fetch and inject the existing
ID/EX bubble. In the following MEM cycle, capture the actual accepted
load result directly into the waiting consumer's ID/EX operands.
Older dmem stalls hold admission until the load really completes; no
speculative load value or additional compulsory load-use bubble is
allowed. Gate MEM forwarding with in.valid, final trap-adjusted
reg_write, and memory-stage acceptance, and use the same load extraction
datapath as MEM/WB. Preserve EX-over-MEM-over-WB priority when several
instructions write the same register, including x0 exclusions.

An ID/EX hold retains its already resolved operands, ALU inputs, and
metadata together. An invalid input or accepted flush clears the whole
bundle, including side-effect controls, as the champion does. Keep
dmem-stall precedence, divider busy draining, held divider results,
and MEM/WB forwarding-data retention; do not add a new stall condition
for ordinary EX-to-ID bypass. A divider captures registered operands
at its accepted launch, and its completing response is the current
EX bypass source for its immediate successor. Prediction correction
still kills a younger instruction at the register boundary, while a
correctly predicted JAL can forward PC+4 to its target instruction.
Branch training occurs once per actual EX advance. Raw fetched bits
and source addresses remain independent of correction, avoiding the
redirect/decode feedback already removed by the champion. No invalid,
trapped, held, or squashed producer can create a bypass write.

Keep multiplication/division arithmetic and every exact ALTOPS formula
unchanged; both real and formal builds exercise the retimed routing.
Preserve nret=1, all top-level IO and RVFI fields, decoder legality,
traps, memory handshakes, and strictly consecutive retirement order.
The expected gain is 20 percent in fitness from higher Fmax without
compulsory extra instruction cycles. A median near 58-60 MHz would
yield roughly 138-143 iterations/sec if cycles stay at the champion
count. Those are predictions, not measured results. The main risk is
that EX-result-to-ID bypass or MEM-load-to-ID extraction becomes the
new critical path; inspect those actual register-to-register paths
and confirm Gowin retains explicit final-operand registers. Run
unchanged formal, unit, and stalled cosimulation gates, then canonical
marker-bounded CoreMark CRC/UART checks and median Gowin timing.
Acceptance requires fitness greater than 120.29, not an Fmax gain alone.

Select advancing EX, completing MEM, or write-first register-file

title: Banked LUT-RAM direction predictor with folded PC indexing
motivation:
The champion's instruction-qualified 128x2 bimodal predictor scores
115.00 at 48.328 MHz and 4,202,272 bracketed CoreMark cycles. It already
avoids most recurring direct-control bubbles. The previous tagged-target
attempt and successful direction-only attempt establish the value of
prediction, while LESSONS.md warns against adding a fetch refill stage
or recovery-to-decode feedback. The remaining opportunity is the physical
direction table: resetting every two-bit counter prevents ordinary
LUT-RAM inference, leaving counter flops, read muxes and reset/write
distribution in the FPGA fabric. Its low-PC-only index also aliases
unrelated branches. Compact banked counter storage and folded PC indexing
can reduce routing pressure and interference without changing fetch latency.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the existing resettable 128-entry direction-counter array with
one banked LUT-RAM bimodal predictor, retaining 128 entries and two-bit
saturating counters. Use the exact seven-bit folded index
fetch_index = PC[8:2] XOR PC[12:6]. Index prediction and EX training
with this same expression, using the accepted instruction's registered
PC for training. Higher PC bits spread branches currently colliding
every 512 bytes. Reference replay of 529,588 canonical CoreMark branches
gives 40,755 misses versus 54,452 for the champion's PC[8:2] index.
Keep direct JAL prediction, instruction-derived targets, sequential
JALR fetch, and all pipeline boundaries intact.

Implement eight explicitly generated banks of sixteen two-bit counters.
Use index[6:4] to select a bank and index[3:0] for its row. Each bank
exposes its counter at the fetch row; select the addressed bank's
completed counter and validity in parallel with the existing PC+4 and
direct-target additions. Store a sixteen-bit initialized/valid vector
per bank in flops. Reset these validity vectors, without resetting the
counter payload arrays. An invalid entry behaves exactly as counter
2'b01, the current weakly-not-taken reset state. Ignore uninitialized
payload bits when invalid in simulation and formal alike. Use portable
asynchronous-read, synchronous-write SystemVerilog arrays; no vendor
primitive, registered lookup, or reset sweep is needed.

Separate validity reset from payload writing so synthesis sees no reset
on the counter memories. On branch_update, select only the addressed
bank and row and set its validity bit. If previously invalid, write
2'b10 for taken or 2'b00 for not taken: these are the exact first
saturating updates from the implied reset value 2'b01. Otherwise read
the current counter at the training row and increment/decrement with
saturation, preserving live-counter update semantics. Simultaneous fetch
and training may address different rows; do not assume one shared read
address or add same-cycle outcome bypass into prediction. Nonblocking
writes become visible after the accepting edge, as in the existing
predictor. Keep the seven-bit branch_index connection and existing
branch_update/outcome signals; no port or bundle expansion is needed.

Preserve instruction qualification, direct-target alignment gating,
saved predicted_taken and instruction-derived direct_target metadata,
direction-XOR EX correction, and resolved RVFI next-PC reporting.
Aliasing may change guesses but cannot redirect non-control or reserved
encodings. Training remains the existing single valid, legal, aligned
conditional-branch EX-to-EX/MEM acceptance event. No training occurs
during reset, bubbles, divider occupancy or dmem holds. Keep correction
priority over younger imem/load-use stalls and full ID/EX control
clearing on squash. Preserve memory handshakes, divider behavior,
forwarding retention, trap checks, nret=1 IO and retirement order.

A temporary prototype of this exact 128-entry, eight-bank design used
3,121 LUTs and 842 flip-flops versus the champion's 3,358 LUTs and 970
flip-flops. Gowin placement options 0/1/2 reported 49.301, 50.676 and
50.676 MHz, giving 50.676 MHz median Fmax. Stalled canonical CoreMark
completed with all five expected CRCs, the validation literal, no OOB
access and MMIO-bracketed timing: start 14,995, stop 4,205,178, or
4,190,183 measured cycles. Their product gives about 120.94 iter/sec,
5.17% above 115.00 and above the 4.6% acceptance bar. The benefit
combines a 4.86% Fmax increase with a 0.29% cycle reduction; the worst
path remains in unchanged ALU/forwarding logic. This is prototype
evidence, not a completed correctness gate: run unchanged formal and
full cosimulation gates, directed predictor tests, CRC validation and
median vendor timing on the final implementation. The acceptance margin
is modest, so preserve concrete banking, reset and indexing structure
rather than expanding capacity or adding unrelated RTL changes.

title: Balance branch comparison logic to shorten EX recovery
motivation:
The current champion scores 162.96 at a median 68.482 MHz with
4,202,272 marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. Registering resolved operands
removed the previous register-file-to-execute timing prefix. A fresh
champion placement-option-0 run reproduces 63.656 MHz and identifies
the 20.783 ns worst path from registered rs2 through the EX branch
comparison carry chain, trap qualification, redirect and ID/EX clear
logic into registered ALU operands. Earlier micro_opt attempts addressed
division, payload squash and multiplier sharing; none shortened the
branch comparator itself.

A local prototype of just the balanced branch comparison tree produces
Gowin Fmax values of 80.108, 78.099 and 78.099 MHz for placement options
0, 1 and 2. Median Fmax improves 14.04 percent to 78.099 MHz. Logic rises
only from 3613 to 3666 LUTs; registers, LUT-RAM, BSRAM and DSP counts
remain 985, 40, 4 and 6. Stalled canonical CoreMark passes CRC/UART and
marker checks with exactly the champion's 4,202,272 cycles, giving
prototype fitness 185.85. The existing 27-test cocotb pipeline suite
and selftest cosimulation with and without bus stalls pass. A Yosys
combinational SAT miter proves the extracted prototype predicates
equal the original six relational predicates and default-false case
for every 32-bit operand pair and all eight branch funct3 values.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the EX branch unit's wide relational operators with an explicitly
balanced comparison tree suited to four-input FPGA LUTs. Preserve the
pipeline boundaries, predictor, exact branch outcomes and all instruction
latencies. This is a local Boolean implementation change to comparison,
intended to raise Fmax while preserving CoreMark iterations per cycle.

Compute equality and unsigned less-than for sixteen independent two-bit
slices of the registered rs1/rs2 operands. Each leaf has four operand
inputs. Combine adjacent low/high groups in four balanced levels using
eq = eq_high & eq_low and
lt = lt_high | (eq_high & lt_low).
Reproduce the measured prototype with packed 31-bit eq/lt node vectors:
leaves occupy indices 15+i for operand slice [2*i +: 2], i=0..15;
internal node n=0..14 combines high child 2*n+2 and low child 2*n+1.
Node zero is the root. This layout keeps the most significant operand
slices on each group's high child.
The root supplies whole-word equality and unsigned less-than. Derive
signed less-than as (rs1[31] ^ rs2[31]) ? rs1[31] : unsigned_less.
Use these shared facts for BEQ/BNE, BLT/BGE and BLTU/BGEU, complementing
only the matching legal predicate; retain false for unsupported branch
funct3 values. Express the tree with static generate indices or explicit
levels so synthesis sees bounded local comparisons rather than a new
32-bit ripple comparator. Do not replace comparison with a full-width
subtractor whose carry propagation recreates the long path.

Keep target alignment faults, branch training on actual acceptance,
direction-XOR correction, EX/MEM and ID/EX hold/flush priorities,
bypass producer validity, divider protocol and RVFI metadata intact.
Preserve nret=1, decoder default-illegal behavior and all correctness
checks. Validate all six branch conditions with equality, differing
signs and differences at every bit position, including misaligned
taken targets and independent instruction/data bus stalls. Run the
unchanged formal and stalled CoreMark gates and inspect vendor timing

Expected gain is 14 percent in fitness, supported by the local prototype

The prototype's new limiting paths cross ALU-result-to-ID forwarding;
leave that separate opportunity for a later hypothesis. Full pipeline
riscv-formal remains an implementation gate; the local SAT proof covers
comparator equivalence and does not replace that gate. Acceptance
requires fitness above 170.46, accounting for the 4.6 percent margin.

title: Register multiply completion outside the ordinary EX bypass path
motivation:
The champion scores 162.96 iter/sec at 68.482 MHz and 4,202,272
marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. LESSONS.md and the structural history
show that isolating division and registering resolved execution inputs
produced large gains, whereas adding a fetch boundary cost branch refill
cycles. After operand retiming, the worst reported path starts at an
ID/EX source register, crosses EX and ID, and ends at a multiplier cell
with 20.783 ns arrival and 39 cells. The same-cycle EX multiply result
still feeds younger ID operand capture. Registering multiply completion
can break this dependency recurrence without slowing every instruction.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion scores 162.96 iter/sec at 68.482 MHz and 4,202,272
marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. LESSONS.md and the structural history
show that isolating division and registering resolved execution inputs
produced large gains, whereas adding a fetch boundary cost branch refill
cycles. After operand retiming, the worst reported path starts at an

with 20.783 ns arrival and 39 cells. The same-cycle EX multiply result
still feeds younger ID operand capture. Registering multiply completion
can break this dependency recurrence without slowing every instruction.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move MUL, MULH, MULHU and MULHSU out of the ordinary combinational ALU
result/bypass cone into one blocking registered multiply unit. Preserve
the existing stage topology and single-cycle ordinary RV32I execution,
instruction-qualified direct prediction, registered final ID/EX operands,
one-bubble load-use interlock and iterative divider. This is one structural
change: a multiply completes from a result register instead of crossing
arithmetic and younger operand selection in the same cycle.

Use request-valid/ready and result-valid/ready handshakes. An accepted
request computes and registers the architectural 32-bit multiply result
directly from the already registered ID/EX operands and operation. Do
not add a redundant operand-capture or preparation cycle. Share one
explicitly sized signed 33-by-33 product: extend a with its sign bit
for MULH/MULHSU and zero otherwise, and extend b with its sign bit only
for MULH. Select product[31:0] for MUL and product[63:32] for high-half
operations before the response register. The low word is independent
of signedness. Ensure unsigned operands are represented as positive
signed 33-bit values and the full product is 66 bits. This arithmetic
organization supports the registered unit; the performance hypothesis
is its register boundary, not sharing alone. No multiplication result
may bypass to ID before that register is valid.

A multiply occupies EX for two cycles in the zero-wait case: launch at
the first edge, then transfer the held registered response into EX/MEM
at the next edge. Thus each multiply adds one compulsory cycle, while
all non-multiply, non-divide instructions retain current throughput.
At launch, snapshot the instruction's execute payload and architectural
RVFI operands. Hold fetch and ID/EX during launch/wait, drain older
MEM/WB work, and insert a fully cleared EX/MEM bubble when not held by
an older dmem request. Keep every side-effect control zero in bubbles.
Older dmem backpressure takes precedence over launch and transfer.
Retain response and saved metadata until transfer is accepted, publish
the final result and destination as the advancing EX bypass source on
that transfer, and resume the immediate dependent instruction then.
Clear unit state on reset. Gate accepted requests, responses and writes
with validity and legal trap-adjusted controls. A held multiply must
never relaunch, retire twice, replay an older store or train a branch.

Extend the existing EX-busy mechanism to multiply occupancy, keeping
the divider's request/response and saved payload independent. Preserve
EX-over-MEM-over-write-first-RF priority, correct x0 behavior, accepted
load extraction, and forwarding on consecutive multiply/divide and
dependent branch, JALR, address and store-data instructions. Branch
recovery still occurs only on EX advance and kills younger side effects;
no extra fetch register or branch refill penalty is introduced.

Remove real multiply operators from the ordinary alu.sv output cone;
real multiply opcodes have deterministic inactive outputs there and
execute only through the registered unit. Preserve the exact ALTOPS
formulas in alu.sv and implement those same formulas in the new unit
through the identical one-register request/response transaction, for
every operand pair. Formal and real builds must exercise the same new
interlock and forwarding behavior. Migrate all existing real multiply
vectors to the new unit suite rather than dropping arithmetic coverage.

A reference replay of the canonical CoreMark ELF counted 93,960
multiplies inside its start/stop markers, equivalent to 2.24 percent
of the champion's measured cycles for a one-cycle penalty. A temporary
prototype of this exact single-register unit and EX integration ran
the unchanged stalled CoreMark harness to completion with all five
expected CRCs, the validation literal and no out-of-bounds access.
Start was cycle 15,107 and stop was 4,311,551, giving 4,296,444
bracketed cycles, only 2.241 percent above the champion. Unchanged
stalled RVFI cosimulation passed selftest and all three random programs
with 115, 11,037, 11,094 and 12,059 retirements respectively.

Gowin place options 0/1/2 for the same prototype reported 85.566,
91.982 and 91.982 MHz, giving a median of 91.982 MHz. Area was 3,708
LUTs, 1,063 flip-flops, 40 LUT-RAM cells, four BSRAMs and two DSPs.
The product of measured Fmax and marker-bounded iterations/cycle is
214.09 iter/sec, 31.37 percent above 162.96 and comfortably above
the 170.45616 acceptance bar. The option-0 worst path decreased from
20.783 to 16.981 ns and now ends at an ID/EX operand register rather
than a multiplier cell. Predict 30 percent fitness gain with medium
confidence, allowing for final implementation and correctness work.
This is prototype evidence, not a completed formal or arithmetic-unit
gate. Preserve the tested one-register latency and blocking integration;
do not introduce extra operand/preparation stages or a result bypass
around the response register. The remaining risks are real high-half
arithmetic corner cases, reset/backpressure interactions, and changes
to physical mapping in the final implementation. Run the unchanged
formal/cosimulation gates, all real arithmetic suites, canonical
CRC/UART validation, existing MMIO markers and median Gowin timing.
Preserve nret=1, all core IO, legality and alignment traps, memory
semantics, retirement order and every hard invariant.

title: Compact banked direction prediction on the operand-retimed champion
motivation:
The current champion scores 162.96 iter/sec at 68.482 MHz and 4,202,272
measured CoreMark cycles. Its bypass-resolved operands are already
registered before EX, but its 128x2 branch direction table still resets
every payload bit and therefore uses counter flops and read multiplexers.
The earlier banked predictor trial scored 125.61 on the older, unretimed
pipeline: it improved its own parent by 9.23%, reduced LUTs from 3,358
to 3,113 and flip-flops from 970 to 842, and reduced CoreMark cycles to
4,190,183. It lost the tournament to the independent operand-retiming
change, rather than demonstrating a regression when combined with it.
Apply the compact predictor to the present retimed champion to reduce
predictor area and routing pressure without reintroducing the older
register-file/forwarding timing path or a fetch refill stage.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only the direction-table implementation with a 128-entry,
two-bit saturating bimodal predictor organized as eight banks of
sixteen rows. Use the same seven-bit index in fetch and EX training:
PC[8:2] XOR PC[12:6]. Select bank with index[6:4] and row with
index[3:0]. Higher PC bits reduce interference between branches that
collide in the current low-PC-only table. Preserve the existing
instruction-qualified conditional prediction and aligned direct JAL
prediction; JALR continues to resolve in EX.

Implement each bank's counter payload as an asynchronous-read,
synchronous-write 16x2 array without reset. Reset only a sixteen-bit
validity vector per bank. A row whose validity is zero behaves as
2'b01, exactly the champion's weakly-not-taken reset value, regardless
of uninitialized payload bits. On the first accepted update, write
2'b10 for taken or 2'b00 for not taken and set validity. Otherwise
saturate the live counter at the training row. Separate payload writes
from validity reset so Gowin can infer small distributed RAMs. Support
simultaneous fetch and training at different rows; do not substitute
the saved prediction for the live update counter or add a combinational
EX-outcome bypass into fetch. No reset sweep or registered lookup.
Compute a combinational next_counter per bank, defaulting to its live
update counter and overriding it with the saturating increment or
decrement. The payload always_ff writes next_counter whenever
!reset && branch_update && branch_index[6:4] selects that bank,
including unchanged saturated values. A separate always_ff resets
validity or marks the updated row valid. Use portable arrays rather
than vendor primitives or RAM attributes.

Keep table lookup parallel with the existing direct-target and PC+4
additions, selecting completed addresses. Keep the exact accepted
predicted_taken bit and instruction-derived direct_target in ID/EX,
direction-XOR recovery, and resolved architectural PC reporting.
Train exactly once on the existing valid, legal, aligned conditional
branch EX advance. Dmem holds, divider occupancy, bubbles and reset
must not update the predictor. Correction retains priority over
younger imem/load-use holds, and ID/EX squash still clears the complete
bundle including memory and register-write controls. Raw instruction
bits and register-file addresses remain independent of correction.
Preserve the current registered rs1_val, rs2_val, alu_a and alu_b and
current EX/MEM bypass interfaces verbatim; do not transplant old
pipeline RTL along with the predictor. All arithmetic, pipeline
boundaries, bus handshakes, trap checks, nret=1 IO and RVFI ordering
remain governed by the existing contract.

An isolated prototype of this exact predictor on the current retimed
RTL gives Gowin placement-option 0/1/2 Fmax values of 66.674, 72.566
and 72.566 MHz, or 72.566 MHz median. Area is 3,438 LUTs, 857 FFs,
56 LUT-RAMs, four BSRAMs and six DSPs, versus the champion's 3,613
LUTs, 985 FFs, 40 LUT-RAMs, four BSRAMs and six DSPs. The worst
option-0 setup path still starts at registered rs2_val and ends at
the multiplier input, with 38 cells and 20.072 ns arrival versus
the champion's 39 cells and 20.783 ns. The physical gain therefore
transfers to the operand-retimed parent rather than depending on
the discarded older pipeline.

Stalled canonical CoreMark completed with all five expected CRCs,
the validation literal, no OOB accesses and valid MMIO timing
brackets: 4,190,183 measured cycles for ten iterations. Median Fmax
times iterations/cycle is 173.181 iter/sec, 6.27% above 162.96 and
above the 4.6% acceptance bar. The cycle reduction is only 0.29%;
most of the gain is the 5.96% Fmax improvement. These are prototype
measurements; the existing pipeline cocotb suite also passed against
the isolated prototype. Formal and complete cosimulation gates have
not been run on this prototype and remain required for implementation.
Preserve the concrete bank,
reset and update structure, re-run pipeline and correctness gates,
and confirm the median vendor-timed product on the final RTL.

title: Restrict ID/EX reset and squash to validity and control
motivation:
The current champion scores 207.55 iter/sec at 89.174 MHz. Its worst path
returns through EX completion and forwarding into ID/EX operand registers.
The current ID register places reset, flush and fetch validity on the entire
wide payload, although invalid instructions are already suppressed by valid
and fully cleared controls downstream. Prior micro_opt work identified this
fanout before operand retiming and registered multiplication. The current
pipeline makes the same local control/data partition promising again.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current champion scores 207.55 iter/sec at 89.174 MHz. Its worst path
returns through EX completion and forwarding into ID/EX operand registers.
The current ID register places reset, flush and fetch validity on the entire
wide payload, although invalid instructions are already suppressed by valid
and fully cleared controls downstream. Prior micro_opt work identified this
fanout before operand retiming and registered multiplication. The current
pipeline makes the same local control/data partition promising again.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Partition the ID/EX register into a narrow reset/squash control bank and a
payload bank that captures on !stall. Remove reset, flush and in.valid from
payload D and enable cones. Keep exactly the existing pipeline stages,
instruction latencies, forwarding, branch prediction and arithmetic units.
This is one micro-optimization: implement cancellation through instruction
control state rather than clearing every associated data bit.

The payload bank contains pc, architectural rs1/rs2 values, final alu_a/alu_b,
imm, rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr, instr, predicted_taken and direct_target. It has
no reset or squash branch: on every !stall edge capture its existing
combinational next values; otherwise hold. It may capture unavailable or
wrong-path fetched bits, but they cannot perform architectural work. Do not
add a flush-over-stall data update or change the existing hazard logic.

Keep ctrl_t and valid in a separate always_ff block with their original
priority: reset or flush clears the complete ctrl_t and valid, even when
stall is asserted; otherwise !stall captures decoded controls and valid
only for an available instruction, and captures ctrl_t='0 and valid=0 for
an unavailable fetch. Otherwise retain controls and validity. Clearing all
side-effect controls, rather than only valid, is essential because some
consumers inspect controls without qualifying them with validity.

A valid instruction always captures every payload field on the same edge
that sets valid. A held valid instruction retains operands and metadata
through load-use, older dmem backpressure and blocking arithmetic. Reset
must still clear all downstream EX/MEM and MEM/WB bundles, arithmetic unit
state, the register file, PC, predictor and retirement order as before.
The existing EX path clears the entire EX/MEM bundle for invalid input;
thus uninitialized or squashed ID data cannot enter memory, bypass, branch
training, requests, or valid RVFI records. Prove this with symbolic initial
payload values and retain every reset and trap assertion. Do not introduce
synthesis don't-cares or relax any test to accept observable X/Z values.

A reset-preserving prototype of the payload/control partition measured
87.538, 92.250 and 92.250 MHz across Gowin placement options, versus the
champion's 83.021, 89.174 and 89.174 MHz. Its median gain was only 3.45
percent, below the 4.6 percent acceptance margin. The proposed refinement
also removes reset from the payload bank, reducing the same control fanout
and muxing further. That added reset removal must be timed and verified;
the earlier prototype does not establish an accepted improvement.

Require unchanged stalled and unstalled RVFI cosimulation, all unit checks,
formal legality/ordering/liveness, canonical CoreMark CRCs and validation
literal, bounded memory accesses and the existing MMIO timing brackets.
CoreMark cycle count should remain exactly 4,296,444 for the supplied
stall sequence. With unchanged cycles, median Fmax must exceed about
93.276 MHz to clear 217.0973 iter/sec. Preserve nret=1, core IO, decoder
default-illegal behavior, trap suppression, arithmetic and all invariants.

implementation_notes:
# Restrict ID/EX reset and squash to validity and control

Implemented the proposed partition in `cores/bench/rtl/id_stage.sv`.
The 272-bit payload captures the existing decode, forwarding and ALU-input
expressions on every `!stall` edge, without a reset, flush or fetch-valid
condition. Otherwise it holds. The complete 22-bit `ctrl_t` and `valid`
remain in a separate sequential block: reset/flush clear both ahead of
stall; an advancing available instruction captures decoded controls and
validity; an unavailable fetch clears both. No pipeline stage, latency,
interlock, arithmetic unit, prediction logic, downstream reset, decoder
behavior or IO was changed. `nret` remains 1.

All existing tests and assertions were retained. Pipeline checks now
monitor complete payload retention during every hold and verify that
invalid ID controls cannot launch arithmetic, forward a write, redirect
or train a branch. Invalid EX/MEM must be entirely zero with no memory
request or forwarding write, and invalid MEM/WB cannot write the RF.
Focused sequences exercise unavailable and wrong-path loads, stores,
MUL/DIV, illegal instructions, branches and JALR, plus reset during
load-use, older-memory and arithmetic holds. They check exact operands,
retirement order, traps, memory events and existing zero-wait latency.

Additional verification-only audits live in `test_pipeline.py` and stage
their harnesses/copies under `TMPDIR`. The Icarus four-state audit starts
with genuinely uninitialized ID data, holds it through reset and then
captures unavailable fetched data. It requires known, inactive side-effect
signals and known downstream/memory outputs. The symbolic audit leaves
initial payload unconstrained and both bus-ready signals, fetched data,
load data and subsequent resets symbolic. Its added assertions check
payload capture/hold, control priority, invalid suppression, retirement
order and full downstream, PC, predictor, RF and arithmetic resets.
The symbolic audit uses ALTOPS; real arithmetic remains checked by the
existing unit tests and cosimulation. No synthesis don't-cares were added.

Local validation:

- Required Verilator lint command: PASS, no warnings.
- Unchanged `RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench JOBS=8 bash formal/run_all.sh`:
  PASS on the first RTL attempt, 53 passed / 0 failed, including legality,
  ordering, liveness and cover. No RTL formal-fix attempts were needed.
- Final `make test TARGET=bench`: PASS, 14 pytest tests in 43.25 seconds,
  including all 12 original runners, both new cocotb sequences, both new
  initial-payload audits and all existing real/ALTOPS arithmetic checks.
- Four-state initial-payload audit: PASS. The initial audit harness needed
  a simulator-compatible reduction-X check; the strict known-output
  requirement was retained.
- Symbolic initial-payload audit: PASS, unbounded SMT induction in SBY
  prove mode with depth 8 and unconstrained initial ID payload. Its initial
  verification-only staging needed a Yosys-compatible explicit payload
  width, and its status parser was adjusted for SBY's `PASS 0 28` format.
  The actual assertions and RTL were unchanged by those harness fixes.
- `make cosim TARGET=bench NRET=1`: PASS, both stalled/unstalled selftest RVFI
  comparisons and stalled CoreMark CRC validation.
- Explicit stalled CoreMark run: `oob=false`, `ebreak=true`,
  `bench_bracketed=true`, start 15,107, stop 4,311,551, exactly 4,296,444
  measured cycles. CRCs: e9f5 / e714 / 1fd7 / 8e3a / fcaf. UART includes
  `Correct operation validated.`
- `make timing TARGET=bench` and all three vendor placement options:
  84.665 / 86.830 / 86.830 MHz; median 86.830 MHz. Option 0 uses 3,734 logic
  cells, 1,090 registers, 40 LUT-RAM, 4 BSRAM and 2 DSP.

Timing concern: median Fmax regressed 2.63% from the 89.174 MHz champion.
With unchanged cycles, predicted fitness is 202.0974 iterations/second,
below the 217.0973 acceptance target (approximately 93.276 MHz). The
reset-removal refinement therefore does not establish an accepted
improvement. Placement 1/2 still have an EX completion/forwarding path
through the divider and forwarding selection to ID ALU operands.

There are no architectural deviations from the hypothesis. The RTL is
left implementing the requested experiment despite its timing regression;
no unrelated optimization or contract/test relaxation was applied.
lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r5s0 (regression, -2.63%): Removing reset/flush/fetch-valid gating from the ID/EX payload leaves the divider-completion/forwarding-to-alu_a/alu_b critical path intact, so reduced control fanout alone can regress Fmax even with unchanged CoreMark cycles.

title: Complete pipelined multiplies in MEM instead of blocking EX
motivation:
The champion reaches 207.55 iter/sec at 89.174 MHz and 4,296,444
marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. Structural history shows that isolating
arithmetic and registering resolved operands helped substantially,
whereas an extra fetch boundary cost branch refill cycles. The latest
reported worst path is 17.339 ns through 11 cells, from the ID/EX
alu_op register through multiply-completion control, EX forwarding and
ID operand capture. The multiplier already registers its answer, but
returning that answer through the blocking EX completion path retains
complicated same-cycle operation qualification and operand selection.
There are 93,960 dynamic multiplies in the canonical measured interval;
independent successors need not pay the current unconditional busy cycle.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the existing one-register multiplier a pipelined EX-to-MEM producer.
Launch a legal multiply exactly when its ID/EX instruction advances into
EX/MEM. Capture the existing execute/RVFI metadata in EX/MEM on that same
edge and the selected architectural product in mul_unit's response
register. MEM consumes these matching registers together, selects the
registered multiply answer as its architectural result, and forwards it
through the existing completing-MEM bypass. Remove multiply responses
from the advancing-EX bypass and remove multiply from blocking EX busy.
Division retains its existing blocking request/response implementation.
This is one structural change to multiply issue and completion ownership;
retain the predictor, fetch topology and ordinary RV32I pipeline latency.

Register explicit multiply and divide operation-class bits with the
decoded ID/EX controls. Use those bits for stage routing and interlocks
instead of rediscovering classes from alu_op on the EX-to-ID feedback
path. Extend the one-bubble load-use rule to an immediately dependent
multiply consumer: an EX multiply has no current EX bypass value, but
the next cycle its registered MEM result can be captured into ID/EX.
Treat multiply dependencies on branch/JALR operands, effective addresses
and store data exactly like other architectural register dependencies.
Preserve EX-over-MEM-over-write-first-RF priority and x0 semantics.
Independent successors advance without a multiply stall; dependent
successors require one bubble, so no instruction requires more multiply
delay than the current implementation in the zero-wait case.

Permit mul_unit to accept a new request on the same edge its previous
response is consumed, giving consecutive independent multiplies one
result per cycle. Request acceptance must be a legal EX advance, response
consumption must be the matching EX/MEM multiply's MEM acceptance, and
their controls must not form a combinational ready/valid loop. A dmem
stall freezes EX/MEM and younger stages and prohibits launch, replacement
and response consumption. Retain the response until its matching MEM
instruction advances. After consumption without replacement clear valid.
Reset clears the response and pipeline state. Capture metadata only in
the existing pipeline registers; remove the redundant saved multiply
execute payload and return-to-EX transfer path. Keep cleared bubbles,
trap-adjusted writes, exact RVFI operands and consecutive retirement order.
Squashed younger multiplies must never issue; older multiplies may finish
while a younger branch corrects fetch or a divider occupies EX.

Preserve the shared signed 33-by-33 arithmetic, low/high result selection,
all four real RV32M multiply semantics and the exact operation-specific
RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS formulas. Both builds use the same pipelined launch,
response ownership, MEM forwarding and dependent-consumer interlock.
The intended gain is a shorter multiply-control-to-ID path and fewer
unnecessary issue bubbles, without an additional pipeline stage or a
branch-refill penalty. Remaining risks are multiplier register mapping,
a new MEM selection path, and result/metadata alignment under stalls.
Validate all real arithmetic suites, unchanged formal and RVFI cosim,
canonical CoreMark CRC/UART/marker checks and median vendor timing.
Preserve nret=1, the complete top-level IO and all hard invariants.

title: Local prediction squash clears control while freeing payload registers
motivation:
The current predictor already avoids recurring direct-control bubbles,
but every EX misprediction still drives a whole-ID/EX zeroing mux. Its
flush and invalid-fetch handling clear PC, instruction, target, operands,
ALU inputs and destination metadata as well as valid and control bits.
Prediction recovery needs to invalidate the instruction and clear every
side-effect control; clearing the inactive payload adds substantial
fanout and input muxing to a timing-sensitive recovery path. Prior BHT
banking changed CoreMark cycles by only 0.29 percent. Reduce the physical
cost of existing predictor recovery instead of adding table complexity.

title: Factor AND OR XOR into one four-input-LUT ALU result family
motivation: The current champion has a 93.817 MHz median Fmax, with the worst timed path crossing the combinational ALU and EX result selection before returning to ID/EX operands. Its ALU treats AND, OR and XOR as three separate full-width output alternatives. Each result bit can instead use one shared four-input Boolean function, reducing the number of wide alternatives in the ALU output mux. Prior payload-reset and predictor-banking attempts left ordinary ALU forwarding as a timing limit; explicit prefix adders and broad forwarding rewrites also failed to improve local vendor timing. This proposal targets only the bitwise ALU family and its result-selection cost.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Implement AND, OR and XOR as one shared bitwise result family without changing latency, the ALU port interface, pipeline topology, operation encoding or forwarding behavior. In parallel with data arrival, decode two scalar controls:
  xor_en = (op == ALU_OR) || (op == ALU_XOR)
  and_en = (op == ALU_OR) || (op == ALU_AND)
For each bit i, compute
  logic_result[i] = ((a[i] ^ b[i]) & xor_en)
                  | ((a[i] & b[i]) & and_en).
This has exactly four independent inputs per bit: a[i], b[i], xor_en and and_en. AND enables only the second term, XOR only the first, and OR enables both, since (a XOR b) OR (a AND b) equals a OR b. For every other operation both enables are zero. Express this as two masked word terms ORed together, allowing Gowin to map each result bit into one LUT4.

Replace the three separate ALU case arms with one grouped ALU_AND, ALU_OR, ALU_XOR arm returning logic_result. Preserve the existing ADD/SUB, signed/unsigned comparisons, three shifts, LUI, default-zero behavior and real inactive M-extension outputs exactly. Keep every RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS operation-specific formula unchanged and use the same bitwise family in both build modes. Do not introduce another full-width bitwise-op selector after the shared result: the grouped arm is the sole insertion point into the existing ALU output selection.

The single micro-optimization is factoring a three-choice 32-bit ALU sub-mux into a LUT4-sized truth table. It should reduce logic/routing pressure and shorten ALU result selection, including selection traversed by non-bitwise results, while preserving the champion's exact instruction schedule and marker-bounded CoreMark cycle count. Decoder validation, x0, trap discipline, bus acceptance, arithmetic ownership, payload stall/squash/reset policy, predictor recovery, nret=1 IO and all RVFI fields/order remain unchanged. No don't-care inputs or relaxed checks are permitted.

With unchanged 4,296,444 measured CoreMark cycles, acceptance requires median Fmax above approximately 98.133 MHz and fitness above 228.405 iter/sec. Validate actual LUT mapping and median timing with Gowin; a Boolean simplification alone is not evidence of a fitness gain. Run the existing normal/ALTOPS ALU suites and unchanged pipeline/formal/stalled cosimulation/CoreMark gates, including canonical CRCs, the validation literal, OOB checks and existing start/stop MMIO brackets.

title: Replace the shared EX bypass bus with direct operand forwarding
motivation:

marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. Its reported worst path is now the
registered alu_a to younger registered alu_b recurrence through the
ALU, EX result selection and ID operand selection: 16.306 ns and ten

source forwarding, x0 gating and immediate/PC selection. The r2s1 fetch
register added 6.45 percent cycles, while r5s1 multiply completion in MEM
improved fitness only 4.24 percent, below the acceptance threshold.
Shortening the existing dependency recurrence without another latency
or issue penalty is the strongest remaining structural opportunity.

Replace the centralized EX-result bypass bus and serial ID input muxes
with an operand-local, one-hot forwarding crossbar feeding the existing
ID/EX registers directly. This is one structural change to result and
operand flow; retain all pipeline boundaries, the predictor, blocking
multiplier/divider timing, load-use interlock and instruction throughput.

EX exports separate raw candidate buses for the ordinary ALU result,
PC+4 link value, registered multiply response and registered divide
response. Export the matching destination and qualified write enable
for each candidate. Ordinary ALU instructions must reach younger
operand registers without first passing through the jump-versus-ALU
and multiply/divide-versus-ordinary shared result muxes. EX/MEM still
captures the same selected architectural result for normal completion.
Removing these muxes from forwarding must not duplicate ALU arithmetic
or alter the actual RV32M units and their exact ALTOPS formulas.

For each raw ID source address, compute mutually exclusive candidate
selects in parallel with result production. Require a nonzero source,
matching nonzero destination, valid producer, permitted trap-adjusted
register write and actual producer advance. The EX class selects must
be mutually exclusive: ordinary ALU versus link versus accepted multiply
versus accepted divide. Completed arithmetic responses use the saved
launch destination and metadata. A load has no EX value. A busy,
invalid, trapped or stalled instruction is never an eligible producer.
MEM is eligible only for its actual accepted architectural result,
including the existing sign/zero-extended load extraction; EX wins
over MEM and MEM wins over the existing write-first register-file read.

Use these early selects directly in balanced mask-and-OR datapaths,
rather than encoding a selection and rebuilding nested priority muxes.
Form rs1_val and rs2_val from the independent candidates for branches,
JALR, store data, divider launch and exact RVFI operand values. Separately

exclusion into the register-source masks before the data network; PC
and immediate values remain available even when the encoded source
field is zero. Balance the reduction so an ALU result passes through
as few LUT levels as possible after arithmetic. All select generation
must be independent of the value being forwarded, apart from the
existing trap qualification for link-producing control transfers.

Keep the champion's complete reset and its split payload/control update
policy: payload holds on stall and captures on advance; flush or an

title: One-bit agree prediction removes the counter training lookup
motivation:
The champion already predicts direct branches and JALs and scores 218.36
iter/sec at 93.817 MHz. Its 128-entry two-bit direction table needs both
a fetch lookup and a live-counter lookup for saturating EX updates.
Prior counter banking and XOR indexing reduced CoreMark cycles by only
0.29 percent and did not beat the operand-retimed champion. Reference
execution counts only 13,735 JALRs among 2,922,016 marker-bounded retired
instructions, making a return stack's cycle benefit too small to clear
the 4.6 percent acceptance margin. Simplifying direction training offers
a more promising predictor-specific reduction in area and routing.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the resettable 128x2 bimodal counters with a resettable 128x1
agree table, retaining the PC[8:2] fetch and training index. A branch's
static bias is its B-immediate sign bit, instr[31]: backward branches
predict taken and forward branches predict not taken. Each entry records
whether the most recently resolved indexed branch agreed with its own
static bias. Reset entries to one, meaning agreement. Predict direction
as bias when the indexed bit is one, or the inverse bias when it is zero.
This reduces destructive aliasing between oppositely biased branches
while halving table state. Its main physical advantage is that training
simply writes (actual_taken == resolved_instruction[31]); it never reads
the old entry, increments, decrements, or tests counter saturation.

Keep the existing instruction qualification, aligned instruction-derived
direct targets, always-taken aligned JAL prediction, sequential JALR,
saved predicted_taken bit, direction-XOR EX correction, pipeline register
boundaries and localized ID/EX squash policy. Evaluate the agreement
lookup and static-bias XOR in parallel with PC+4 and direct-target adders,
then select completed addresses. Do not add a same-cycle EX-training
bypass to fetch, another prediction stage, cached targets or speculation
state. A table collision changes only a conditional direction guess.

Export the resolved branch's immediate sign from EX and wire it to IF
alongside the existing branch_update/index/outcome signals. Train once
on the existing valid, legal, aligned conditional EX acceptance event;
never train during reset, dmem holds, arithmetic occupancy or bubbles.
Preserve architectural branch_outcome for debug and verification, and
derive agreement only at the predictor write. Nonblocking table writes
become visible after the accepting edge. Use the actual fetched
instruction's bias for prediction and the registered resolving
instruction's bias for training; younger imem bits must not train EX.

Preserve correction priority over younger imem/load-use stalls, complete
control/valid/predicted_taken clearing on squash, payload retention under
stalls, real RV32M arithmetic and ALTOPS behavior, decoded trap rules,
wrong-path side-effect suppression, nret=1 IO, consecutive RVFI order
and resolved architectural pc_next. Do not change arithmetic, forwarding,
memory handshakes, benchmark or evaluation files.

Expect roughly six percent higher fitness primarily from lower predictor
state and elimination of the training read/mutate cone, with a small
accuracy cost possible because there is no two-bit hysteresis. Compare
marker-bounded canonical CoreMark cycles and median Gowin Fmax with the
champion; the product must exceed 228.40456 iter/sec. Validate exact
RVFI PC sequences, opposite-bias aliasing, loop exits/re-entry, reset,
stalled training and wrong-path stores, then unchanged formal/cosim
gates, all canonical CRCs, the validation literal and MMIO brackets.

title: Align M operation codes to shorten EX class selection
motivation: The champion scores 218.36 iter/sec at 93.817 MHz and 4,296,444 marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. Its ALU/EX-to-ID recurrence remains the timing limit. Other placements and local prototypes expose paths from registered alu_op bits through EX completion, forwarding eligibility and younger operands. The current MUL codes 11..14 and DIV/REM codes 15..18 straddle binary boundaries, so EX recognizes each family with four full five-bit equality checks. Prior bitwise factoring, a broad operand crossbar and predictor simplification regressed timing. Local decoded-shifter, comparator and added-class-register experiments also failed to clear the required margin. A compact internal encoding attacks the repeated class decisions without a wider crossbar or extra state.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Recode only the eight internal M-extension ALU tags into a naturally aligned block, retaining all RV32I tags 0..10 and the five-bit tag width:
  MUL=16, MULH=17, MULHSU=18, MULHU=19,
  DIV=20, DIVU=21, REM=22, REMU=23.
These values are {2'b10, instruction_funct3} for the eight validated RV32M instructions. Multiply is exactly alu_op[4:2]==3'b100 and division/remainder is exactly alu_op[4:2]==3'b101. Replace the two EX four-way full-tag classifiers with those bounded three-bit comparisons. Preserve explicit whole-family matching: bit 4 alone must not classify undefined tags 24..31 as M operations.

Keep decoder opcode/funct validation and default-illegal behavior unchanged; its existing symbolic ALU constants now produce the new tags. Keep every other consumer symbolic, including ordinary ALU dispatch, exact ALTOPS formulas, multiplier signedness/high-half selection and divider operation selection. The natural low bits also expose DIV/REM signedness and remainder selection to synthesis through the existing constant comparisons, without changing their arithmetic or request/response protocols. title: Pipeline full-width multiply completion with registered execution classes
motivation:
The champion scores 218.36 iter/sec at 93.817 MHz and 4,296,444 marker-bounded CoreMark cycles. Registered multiplication previously gained 27.36 percent by breaking the multiply-to-ID recurrence. The r5s1 pipelined multiply attempt recovered independent issue slots but gained only 4.24 percent against its then-champion, below acceptance. It predates the champion's improved ID/EX payload/control squash policy. The r6s1 broad forwarding crossbar lost 6.40 percent, so expanding ordinary operand selection is poor evidence for another attempt. Target the multiplier's completion boundary and operation ownership instead.

An isolated full-product-to-MEM prototype on the current champion, with a decoded multiply bit but the old divide-class comparisons, produced Gowin placement-option Fmax values of 87.074, 93.422 and 93.422 MHz, with 3,673 LUTs and two DSPs. Its worst paths remain registered rs2 through EX into BHT updates. Other isolated structural probes exposed alu_op-to-multiply/divide-to-stage-acceptance paths. These are partial-prototype observations, not evidence that the final proposal passes the acceptance threshold.
